titleEn: Isolated Mid-Shaft Femur Fracture - Traction Splint and Three-Drug Analgesia

patient.name: Jordan Ellis
patient.affectEn: alert and oriented but shouting with pain; lying supine mid-field holding his right thigh, which is obviously angulated and swollen; keeps the leg perfectly still
patient.speechEn: loud, short answers between groans of pain; cooperative and answers every question that is asked, but volunteers nothing

scene.settingEn: Grass soccer pitch in Kamloops, 1420 hrs. Dry, sunny, 24 degrees C. Play has stopped and both teams are back on the benches. The patient lies supine mid-field holding his right thigh, which shows obvious mid-shaft angulation and swelling. The cot has to come about 60 metres across grass. One patient. Hospital is 18 minutes away.
hazardsEn: no significant hazards: play has stopped and both teams are on the benches
uneven grass for the 60 m cot carry
open field, dry and sunny, 24 degrees C

bystanders.knowsEn: saw the tackle: an opponent's knee drove into the outside of his right thigh; he dropped straight away; he did not hit his head and did not lose consciousness; they have kept him still and nobody has moved the leg; willing to bring the cot, clear the carry route or hold the leg exactly as directed
kept him still since the tackle; nothing else to add; can help carry the cot across the field and clear the route if asked

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: Sager traction splint with ankle harness, thigh strap and elasticized straps
Entonox cylinder with demand valve and mouthpiece
PCP oral analgesia kit: acetaminophen and ibuprofen tablets
oxygen kit with nasal cannula and non-rebreather mask
spinal immobilization equipment (hard collars, spinal device)

dispatchEn: 1420 hrs. Code 3 to a soccer pitch in Kamloops. 19-year-old male, tackled hard during a game, obvious deformity of the right thigh. Coaches have kept him still. Hospital is 18 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: he is conscious and screaming in pain; no other players injured; there is a first-aid attendant on the field.
arrivalEn: Play has stopped and both teams are back on the benches. The field first-aid attendant waves you over to mid-field: "He did not hit his head and he did not black out. We have kept him still." The cot will have to come about 60 metres across the grass. Dry, sunny, 24 degrees C. One patient.
firstLookEn: Young male supine mid-field, shouting in severe pain and holding his right thigh, which is obviously angulated and swollen at mid-shaft. No blood through his shorts.

primary.locEn: Alert and oriented; shouting with pain but able to answer appropriately. (AVPU = A.)
primary.airwayEn: Open and clear - he is shouting and talking in sentences. Nothing in the mouth.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 24, regular, equal chest rise; no respiratory distress, no accessory muscle use. SpO2 98% on room air if checked now.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 112, strong and regular. No external bleeding anywhere.
primary.rbsEn: Head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, back (as far as can be felt without moving him), left leg and both arms: no injuries. No head, neck or back pain; no head strike, no loss of consciousness, no midline neck tenderness, not intoxicated. RIGHT THIGH (when exposed): closed mid-shaft femur fracture with obvious angulation and a swollen, tense thigh; skin intact, no bleeding. Distal: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses PRESENT, sensation intact, he can wiggle his toes. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: pink, warm, dry. (Examiner note, never volunteer: NEXUS negative - spinal immobilization is not indicated; isolated injury, no shock = STABLE.)

history.ccEn: My leg! My right thigh - I heard it crack. It is broken.

opqrst.oEn: Sudden - the second it happened. A guy's knee drove into the outside of my thigh at full speed, at about 2:14 this afternoon. I heard a crack and went straight down.
opqrst.pEn: Nothing helps. Any movement is agony.
opqrst.rEn: It stays in my thigh - it does not go anywhere, no back or hip pain. Nothing relieves it. I have never hurt that leg before.

history.painScoreEn: 10/10 before analgesia; 4/10 after analgesia and splinting (vitals set 2).

sample.sEn: My right thigh. Nothing else hurts - I did not hit my head, I did not black out, my neck and back are fine.
sample.aEn: No allergies - none to Advil, Tylenol or anything else.
sample.mEn: No medications. I have not taken anything for pain today, and I am not on blood thinners.
sample.pEn: Nothing - I am healthy. No bleeding problems, no liver or stomach problems.
sample.lEn: Pasta and a sports drink at 1230 - about two hours ago.
sample.eEn: We were playing a game and a guy tackled me hard - his knee drove into the outside of my right thigh. I heard a crack and dropped. I have not moved the leg since.

fe.generalEn: I am fit - I play all the time. No recent illness.
fe.cnsEn: I did not hit my head. No dizziness. No numbness or tingling in my foot.
fe.respiratoryEn: No shortness of breath. No asthma.
fe.cardiovascularEn: My heart is racing - it is the pain.
fe.giGuEn: No belly pain. I have never had ulcers or any stomach bleeding.
fe.integumentaryEn: No cuts - the skin over my thigh is not broken.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: Just my right thigh. I have never broken a bone before.
fe.eentEn: No face injury, no ear problems. I have not been scuba diving or anything like that.

findings.headNeckEn: No injury to the head or face. No midline neck tenderness or pain.
findings.chestLungsEn: No injury. Clear and equal air entry at all 6 sites.
findings.backEn: No tenderness or deformity on a careful check.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Hips and pelvis: no tenderness, stable. RIGHT thigh: mid-shaft angulation, swelling and shortening; closed (skin intact). Right foot: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses present, sensation intact, toes move - the same as the left foot. LEFT leg: normal, CSM intact. After the traction splint and at every recheck: distal pulses, sensation and toe movement still present.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: No injury. Circulation, sensation and movement intact in both hands.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: after analgesia and traction splinting (pain 4/10); does not unlock without Entonox

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: The patient screams in pain as the leg is handled and grabs at your arms.
As the traction comes off, the thigh shortens and angulates again and the patient screams in pain.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge; plan traction splint, analgesia kit (acetaminophen, ibuprofen, Entonox), oxygen and cot
Anticipate a painful isolated long-bone injury where analgesia comes BEFORE splinting
triggers: pain relief before we move him

expected.actionEn: Verbalize hazards (none significant), environment (open field, 60 m carry), MOI (direct blow to the thigh, no head strike), one patient
triggers: mechanism is a direct blow to the thigh

expected.actionEn: Don gloves and eye protection
First look: young male supine, in severe pain, obvious mid-thigh deformity, no bleeding through the shorts
Assess LOC / AVPU: Alert
Question sufficiently to rule OUT c-spine using NEXUS criteria and verbalize the reasoning
Assess airway
triggers: he is talking so the airway is patent

expected.actionEn: Assess breathing
Assess circulation; note tachycardia is from pain, with no other shock signs
triggers: rate and quality of the pulse

expected.actionEn: Rapid body survey; expose the thigh, manually stabilize the limb and check distal circulation, sensation and function
Note skin: pink warm dry - important evidence against shock in a femur fracture
triggers: no signs of shock in the skin

expected.actionEn: Verbalize the oxygen decision: SpO2 98% with no distress, so titrate and no supplemental oxygen is required
Keep supine with the injured leg in line with the body, supported manually
triggers: leg in line with the body

expected.actionEn: Categorize correctly as non-RTC and justify it (no shock, distal pulses present, isolated injury)
Ready to load within 30 minutes while still working with purpose
triggers: let us get him on the cot

expected.actionEn: Delegate the field attendant and coaches: bring the cot to the patient, clear the carry route, hold manual traction as directed
Establish chief complaint: severe right thigh pain and deformity
Full OPQRRRST for the pain plus mechanism detail and a specific head/neck/back screen
Obtain a 0-10 pain score before analgesia
PMHx incl liver disease, GI bleeding and bleeding disorders (analgesia contraindications)
Medications - specifically anticoagulants and any acetaminophen or ibuprofen taken in the last 4-6 hours
Allergies - specifically NSAID and acetaminophen sensitivity
LOI with time and content
GCS with components
BP by auscultation - baseline required before Entonox and before splinting
Pulse rate/strength/rhythm
Respirations rate/depth/character
Skin hands-on - confirms the absence of shock
Pupils
SpO2 including oxygen saturation before Entonox use, as the guideline requires
triggers: does the oximeter match the pulse

expected.actionEn: FE - General health
FE - CNS (distal neuro symptoms)
FE - Respiratory (asthma/COPD screen before Entonox)
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU (ulcer and GI bleed screen before ibuprofen)
FE - Integumentary (open vs closed fracture)
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT
Head/neck exam confirming NEXUS-negative status
Chest exam with 6-site auscultation
Abdomen exam
Back exam
triggers: run my hand down the back

expected.actionEn: Lower extremities incl hips/pelvis and documented distal CSM in the injured leg, compared with the uninjured side
Upper extremities with CSM
Initiate the Pain Management protocol with baseline vitals complete and contraindications ruled out for each drug
triggers: can you hold the mouthpiece yourself

expected.actionEn: Give analgesia BEFORE any movement, realignment or splinting - delaying Entonox until after fracture management is a 100% error
triggers: pain relief before we move the leg
wait for the Entonox to work

expected.actionEn: Administer the drugs with the 6 rights (PCP: acetaminophen 1000 mg PO + ibuprofen 400 mg PO + Entonox; EMR: Entonox, cylinder inverted 3 times)
triggers: breathe on this when the pain is bad

expected.actionEn: Apply the traction splint by STAPLES with the correct traction weight (10 percent of body weight, maximum 15 lbs for a closed fracture) and never release it
Reassess distal circulation, sensation and function before and after splinting and after every move
triggers: can you feel me touching your foot

expected.actionEn: Apply cold appropriately (10 minutes on, 5 minutes off) without impairing distal circulation
Reassess ABCs and all interventions after each major move
Second full set of vitals within the non-RTC interval
Reassess and correct traction with every movement and every set of vitals
Reassess the pain score and continue Entonox to effect
Notify the receiving facility
Complete hand-off with analgesia times and doses, traction weight and neurovascular status
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes

specialEvents.descriptionEn: fracture management actually performed on the right thigh: the traction splint is applied with traction pulled (ankle harness on and traction set), OR the angulated thigh is straightened, manipulated or put under manual traction. Record it at the moment it is DONE, never when it is planned or announced ("I will give Entonox before I splint" is not this event). Supporting the leg where it lies, cold packs, padding, sizing the splint beside the leg and distal CSM checks are NOT this event.

traction set above 15 lb, or clearly above 10% of his body weight (he weighs about 120 lb, so about 12 lb is correct); also record it if the candidate uses the open-fracture maximum or no measured traction at all
candidate releases, removes or reduces the traction after it has been applied (correcting it back to the set amount during a reassessment is NOT a release)

candidate applies the traction splint without checking distal pulses, sensation and movement in the right foot first, or after applying it moves on (packaging, lifting, history, transport) without rechecking distal pulses, sensation and movement
candidate applies a hard collar or immobilizes this NEXUS-negative patient on a spinal device / with spinal precautions (manual head support while asking the NEXUS questions is NOT this event)
candidate gives Entonox without verbalizing inverting the cylinder (3 times) before use
PCP gives acetaminophen outside 500-1000 mg PO or ibuprofen outside 300-400 mg PO, or by a route other than PO
cold pack placed directly on bare skin, wrapped so tightly that it could impair distal circulation, or applied without the 10-minutes-on / 5-minutes-off cycle being verbalized
candidate applies supplemental oxygen by non-rebreather or nasal cannula while SpO2 is 98% on room air with no distress, without a titration rationale (the Entonox mouthpiece is NOT oxygen therapy)
candidate lets or asks the patient to sit up, stand, bear weight or walk at any point in the call

drugs.doseEn: inhalation, self-administered through the demand valve; titrate to effect; invert the cylinder 3 times before use; give BEFORE any realignment or splinting
drugs.contraindicationsEn: inability to comply; inability to ventilate an enclosed treatment area; decompression sickness; altered level of consciousness; pneumothorax; air embolism; inhalation injury; nitroglycerin in the last 5 minutes
drugs.cautionsEn: shock; abdominal distention; depressant drugs; COPD; facial injuries

drugs.doseEn: 1000 mg PO (guideline range 500-1000 mg PO; may repeat once after 4 hours)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: hypersensitivity; severe hepatic impairment or severe active liver disease; acetaminophen within the past 4 hours; suspected overdose

drugs.doseEn: 400 mg PO (guideline range 300-400 mg PO; may repeat every 4-6 hours)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: hypersensitivity to ibuprofen or other NSAIDs; active GI hemorrhage or ulcers; pregnancy; anticoagulants

examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You looked at the right leg during your rapid body survey - what did you find?

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR performs the same traction splint and the same sequencing, but analgesia is Entonox only - acetaminophen and ibuprofen are not in EMR scope. The Appendix A pain-management weightings that involve the oral agents therefore do not apply to EMR; what still applies in full is giving Entonox BEFORE fracture management. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP uses the full three-drug ladder: acetaminophen 500-1000 mg PO and ibuprofen 300-400 mg PO on-boarded early (they take 30-60 minutes to work), with Entonox covering the splinting itself. PCP also completes the 9-system Functional Enquiry. IV access is not required for an isolated stable femur fracture with no shock.

sourcePages: scenario tr-08 (data/practical/scenarios.json); BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7-8 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (none met: one long-bone fracture, distal pulses present, no shock), p.11 Primary Survey interventions (stabilizing fractures; realigning limb fractures that are grossly deformed or pulseless), p.21 Musculoskeletal Injuries (check distal pulses and reassess throughout; apply cold; provide analgesia prior to movement in stable patients; apply traction if appropriate; immobilize the joints above and below), p.23 Fracture Management - Traction Splint (indication: suspected mid-shaft femur fracture in a stable patient; assess distal circulation, sensation and function; cold 10 minutes on / 5 off; analgesia if not contraindicated; supine, leg in line; STAPLES; closed mid-shaft: 10% of body weight to a maximum of 15 lbs (7 kg), open: maximum 5 lbs; once traction is applied do NOT release it; reassess and correct traction with each movement and each set of vitals), p.25 Spinal Management (NEXUS / Canadian C-Spine), p.58 Acetaminophen (500-1,000 mg PO; contraindications incl. severe liver disease and acetaminophen within 4 hours), p.65 Entonox (contraindications; before use: primary survey, pain severity, baseline vitals incl. SpO2, history and exam to rule out contraindications; invert cylinder 3 X), p.68 Ibuprofen (300-400 mg PO; contraindications incl. NSAID hypersensitivity, active GI hemorrhage or ulcers, anticoagulants); EMALB Practical Examination Grading Criteria: Fracture Management (not applying the Sager splint to a non-Priority femur fracture when indicated; incorrect amount of traction; does not assess distal circulation or function; ice 10 min on / 5 min off) and Appendix A (Pain Management weighting, handled by the engine)
